utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-95-14/2-A --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Prosecution, Mr. Norman Farrell, Mr. Fabricio Guarglia, and Mr. Wolfgang Sakulin is the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Farrell. For Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my name is Mitko Naumovski, a lawyer from Zagreb, and I am Defence counsel for Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. For Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, representing Mario Cerkez, Bozidar Kovacic, lawyer from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Dario Kordic, are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? THE APPELLANT KORDIC: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you for your question. Yes, I do understand everything on the agenda today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. And Mario Cerkez, are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? THE APPELLANT CERKEZ: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I don't hear because the channel is not adjusted properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He needs his channel adjusted. I finally got it on the transcript. Now, are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand, sir? THE APPELLANT CERKEZ: [Interpretation] I understand you, Your Honour, but I do not -- I'm not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we'll have that fixed up. You sit down, please, sir. Thank you. THE APPELLANT CERKEZ: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems that nobody is receiving Croatian channel, at least on this part of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think in this courtroom the B/C/S/ is channel 6. We'll wait and see whether they can fix it for us. This is a Status Conference called in accordance with the provisions of Rule 65 ter. Now, are there any matters relating to -- Sorry. 65 bis. -- relating to the physical or mental condition of the accused that either wants to raise before we turn to the outstanding matters for the hearing of the appeal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Mr. Kordic has no issues it wishes to raise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. What about on behalf of Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we also have no problems regarding these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, now, I have signed a decision authorising Mr. Kordic's -- I'm sorry -- Mr. Cerkez's reply brief to exceed the page limit, and we've got the usual "me too" application from Mr. Kordic. What is the Prosecution's attitude towards that one, Mr. Farrell?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection, Your Honour. My apologies. The same as the previous one. The Prosecution has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We will make an order accordingly. Now, before we leave this question of replies, I hope that counsel for the two appellants will understand that we do have their appellants' briefs and they are being read and there is no need to repeat what you said in there in response to what the Prosecution has put in its response. We really are able to deal with things by going back to see whether they have been dealt with in your motion, and it is unnecessary for you to keep repeating the same thing over and over again. And particularly, I hope that each of you counsel for the appellants will stick to the particular brief that you are filing your reply in. Counsel for Mr. Cerkez put forward the rather extraordinary proposition that counsel -- every counsel would be likely to take advantage of any document that he's filing to raise issues in relation to anything he wants to, whether it's relating to the particular motion or the particular appeal in question. Now, that, with all due respect, is not the way in which the system will work. You will have plenty of opportunity at the hearing of the appeal to deal with anything you want to orally, and if you do file -- include within a document you file matters relating to some other proceeding, such as the Prosecution appeal, and you put something in your reply -- in your -- I'm sorry. I'll start that again. If you are dealing with your own appeal, in your reply to the Prosecution's appeal, it may well be missed. I confess to having a fairly logical mind and I have read through the documents relating to each of them and I read them separately. If you deal with one issue in a different proceeding, it may not be noticed and you may well find that it's overlooked. So please try to keep to the point of the particular proceedings in which you're filing a document. Now, Mr. Farrell, there has been a problem that has arisen which I should draw to everyone's attention. I am involved in the trial of the three Muslim generals, and in some correspondence which counsel for one of the accused there is having with a trial attorney in that matter, it seems that the Sarajevo archive, if that's the correct expression, in any event, the documents which were taken between the 11th and the 19th of October, 2000, are about to be returned to the ABiH. Now, if that's so, it's going to be very difficult, in the light of the promise which the Prosecution has made, to voluntarily disclose that material to the appellants in this case if we rule that there is a legitimate forensic purpose for them seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If I may respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: My understanding is that the Prosecution will be sending back copies of the documents from the -- what's called the Sarajevo collection, that the originals will remain with the Prosecution, that that is ongoing right now and should be fulfilled shortly. If Your Honour is of the view that to comply with the order -- I mean, sorry, to fulfil the request of the Defence counsel, the Court wishes to request that copies of the documents which have been given over -- we still have the documents in our possession, the originals. We are just sending back the copies. And that's a normal practice, as I'm sure you're aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I know the Prosecution, once they have something, don't like giving out documents to anybody, but these are documents which were seized pursuant to a search warrant and the letter signed by a Ms. Cynthia Fairweather quite clearly says the material will be returned but copies will be made of anything which the three Muslim general accused persons wish to have copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It says quite clearly in this letter the material will be returned but copies will be made for anything that the three Muslim generals, whose names I haven't quite got round to learning how to pronounce, if they need copies of anything, they will have copies made before the material is returned. Now, if you say the originals have been kept and only copies are being sent back, that's quite different to what Ms. Fairweather is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I made a mistake, Your Honour. I read the letter as the Prosecution envisages that copies of the documents that were taken in the archives will be taken back on or around the 19th of October. That's the way I read the letter, and I confirmed with the trial team for Hadzihasanovic that we will retain the originals, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are better at pronunciation of the name than I am. I haven't had the chance to practice it. Anyway, I don't read it that way, but if that's the way it was intended, then we are safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's my understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's good. Now, we recently received from the two appellants their arguments as to whether there is a legitimate forensic purpose, and Mr. Farrell, I hope that the Prosecution will take a slightly better attitude towards the arguments put, whether they be good or bad, than has already been disclosed in the document which was filed on the 2nd of August. That's the explanation for the fact that these documents weren't disclosed earlier, the very long one with Mr. Reid's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Paragraphs 38 and 39, they are demonstrating how they, you say, these documents could not possibly be exculpatory, and you latch on to one of them. "All correspondence from January 1st, 1990 through to March 1994 between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Milosevic," and the response reads this: "Not only is part of the time period of this request, that is, from January 1st, 1990, outside the time frame of the indictment, but it is also -- but it is outside the temporal jurisdiction of the Tribunal." Now, that really must be one of the most absurd answers I have read for a very long time. What happens if Mr. Milosevic wrote a letter to Mr. Izetbegovic back at the beginning of 1990 and said this is what we propose to do and we would be happy if you could start up a war for us to enable us to take over the Croat area?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Certainly if there was material in there, as you suggest, there's no doubt that the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, why put that as an answer? It is totally not an answer. Merely because the document might be outside the time frame of the indictment and precedes the jurisdictional limits of this Tribunal has nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: With respect, I completely understand. I accept your comment. The issue is, with respect -- I accept what you're saying that the very nature of its time frame may in of and of itself not determine its exculpatory nature, clearly. The way it was meant - and I apologise, it was inartfully worded - is that absent any showing that there is some any relevance to the document, this may be another factor that you would consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's another matter, but what concerns me in this matter is what appears to have got out of control at the trial in this constant bickering between counsel for each party, both sides taking smart points on each other, seems to have crept in here, and it's not really very appropriate. Now, the Prosecutor often puts forward the submission that the Prosecution counsel are ministers of justice. That phrase, if you look into the history of it, is directed solely to the obligation of a Prosecution to reveal material to the Defence, and the basis of it, of course, is very clear, because the Prosecution has the better opportunity of obtaining information, and that without such an obligation by the Prosecution, very few defendants would be able to fight the case fairly. That's a situation which is exacerbated in the international field in which we work, because you have got the power to go in and seize documents there which the Defence doesn't have. Now, there are all sorts of arguments about equality of arms about documents which have yet to be resolved. My preferred view is: Is there a legitimate forensic purpose? And I hope that when the Prosecution is giving us their response to the material that came in the other day, that they will look at it as a minister of justice and without taking points like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you for your observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I just thought the time has come to try and spike this constant bickering or point-taking before it gets too bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you for your comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, now, is there anything else that either side wants to raise? Very well. Well, we'll make that order in favour of Mr. Kordic, that he's got the additional pages. It's probably too late to make any observations about it in this case, but that practice direction, to my view, is of assistance only where it manages to restrain parties from putting in hundreds and hundreds of pages. If you go over a few, I don't think there's going to be any problem. Very well, then. Thank you for your attendance. I'll now adjourn.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
